What Happened?
Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) closed at $307.49 on October 2, 2026, up 5.18% during a broad rally in chip and tech stocks. That left shares up 181% year to date and above the Street's mean target of around $289. They remain below the $322.90 close of September 21. That day's chip rally, which coverage linked to Meta Platforms' (META) Muse AI agent, lifted Meta 11.4% and Arm 17.2%, though Meta has not said whose processors run Muse.
Behind the run sits a quieter shift. Royalties brought in $715 million of Arm's $1.29 billion in revenue for the June quarter, results Arm reported on July 29 and posted in its investor relations materials. The new AGI CPU, however, earns a fraction of royalty margins.
A Doubled 2031 Forecast Meets High-30s Gross Margins
As of October 4, consensus revenue for fiscal 2031, which ends in March 2031, stood around $26 billion, up from around $12 billion at the end of 2025. The analysts covering that year rose from 3 to 11 over the same span, so the two averages are not like-for-like. On the July 29 call, an analyst cited $15 billion of AGI CPU revenue expected for fiscal 2031. CEO Rene Haas said Arm is "not changing the numbers at all," adding that its March market-size view "may have been conservative."
Those chips earn far less per dollar of sales. Jason Child, Arm's Chief Financial Officer, said first-generation AGI CPU gross margin should be "somewhere in the high 30% range, maybe low 40s percent," with 50% expected over "the next couple of years." Street estimates show Arm's gross margin falling from 98.2% in fiscal 2026 to around 70% in fiscal 2031. Normalized net margin is still forecast to rise from 38.4% to around 44%. In other words, the Street is counting on operating leverage to absorb a roughly 28-point gross margin drop.
Nvidia's Agent Watchdog Runs on Arm Server Cores
The royalty side shows up in less obvious places. On September 28, Nvidia (NVDA) launched its Open Agent Safety Platform, with Arm among its backers. Its Sentry watchdog, offered as a reference design, runs on BlueField-4 data processing units.
BlueField-4, unveiled in 2025, swaps BlueField-3's up to 16 Cortex-A78 cores, a design typically marketed for smartphones, for a 64-core Grace CPU built on Arm's server-grade Neoverse V2. The platform's OpenShell software can also run on Intel (INTC) x86 systems, and Arm does not disclose what it earns per DPU.
Child pointed to that pocket on the call: "This is being driven by the continued ramp of Arm-based server chips at all the major hyperscalers alongside increasing deployments of data center networking chips, particularly DPUs and SmartNICs where Arm technology is deployed in nearly all leading products." Neoverse shipments passed 1.5 billion cores, with the latest 500 million arriving in 9 months versus 6 years for the first 1 billion.
Higher memory prices pushed Child's fiscal 2027 royalty growth estimate to "closer to the high teens" from about 20%, and Q2 royalty growth is guided to 13%. He expects royalties back "in that 20% range next year and beyond."

What Happened?
Arm Holdings (ARM) fell 7.88% on September 24 to close at $306.34, and the drop had more to do with Arm than the flat market around it. The Nasdaq finished the session essentially unchanged, so this was not a broad growth-stock selloff. Two Arm-specific pressures did the work: a retracement of the stock's roughly 15% Meta Muse spike from September 21, and renewed focus on a CFO share sale disclosed days earlier, both landing on a valuation priced for perfection at more than 300 times trailing earnings.
What makes this drop different from the selloffs earlier in the year is who else is now exposed to it. Days before, on September 18, SoftBank increased a margin loan backed by its Arm shares to $25 billion from $20 billion. Arm's majority owner has tied its own borrowing capacity to Arm's share price, so a stock already priced for perfection now carries a second sensitivity that has nothing to do with royalties or AI chips.
SoftBank Turned Arm's Price Into Its Own Collateral
SoftBank owns about 86% of Arm, and it is funding an enormous AI spending campaign, anchored by a multibillion-dollar investment in OpenAI. To raise cash without selling Arm stock, it has leaned on a margin loan secured by that stake, and this month it renegotiated the facility up to $25 billion, as first reported byBloomberg. Lenders reportedly offered more than SoftBank sought, a sign banks are comfortable taking Arm shares as collateral at current prices.
Margin loans carry loan-to-value limits, so a sharp drop in the collateral can shrink the borrowing base or trigger a call that forces selling. That creates a feedback loop the stock did not have a year ago: an Arm decline pressures SoftBank's funding math, which can invite more selling, which pressures Arm again. It changes nothing about the operating business, but it adds technical fragility on top of an already extreme valuation. The governance backdrop adds to the unease, with proxy advisers ISS and Glass Lewis both recommending a vote against a plan that could pay CEO Rene Haas up to $800 million if Arm reaches a $2 trillion valuation.
In its most recent quarter (fiscal Q1 2027, reported July 29), revenue rose 22% year-over-year to a record $1.29 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.45 beat both guidance and the $0.40 Street estimate. Data center royalty revenue more than doubled year-over-year again, and Neoverse cores have crossed 1.5 billion shipped, the most recent 500 million in nine months against six years for the first billion.
The order book behind the new AGI CPU, Arm's first in-house data center chip, now exceeds $2 billion against $1 billion of committed supply, and management says confidence in beating that $1 billion has risen. Getting the chips built is the harder part. CEO Rene Haas described the constraint bluntly on the July call: "It is a very, very, very tight market across everything, whether it's memory, whether it's test equipment, whether it's substrates, whether it's TSMC wafers." That tightness is why the pipeline outruns bookable revenue, and it delays the exact chip sales the valuation counts on.
The other soft spot is smartphones. Higher memory prices are squeezing handsets, and CFO Jason Child walked full-year royalty growth down toward the high teens from roughly 20%. The mature business is cooling just as the growth business inflects. The CFO share sale that traders fixated on was routine: a pre-scheduled Rule 10b5-1 disposal worth about $3.12 million that left Child with more than 150,000 shares.
Even after the drop, Arm trades near 312 times trailing earnings and about 128 times forward earnings, aprice-to-earnings ratio unmatched in its group, against a semiconductor peer set whose forward P/E averages roughly 67 times on TIKR's Competitors page. Rambus sits near 31 times, and even fast-growing Global Unichip trades near 108. Arm is priced as a separate asset class, and that price is a forecast about the next five years.
The one piece of support is that the Street's mean target of $288.71 now sits just below the market price, a reversal from the summer when the stock traded far above it. Over the past year, that configuration has tended to mark resets rather than tops. Whether it repeats depends on execution Arm has promised but not yet put in the income statement, and the stock now has to clear both the valuation bar and the leverage overhang at once.

Qualcomm is taking Arm to trial again, with billions in royalties at stake
Qualcomm alleges Arm withheld chip testing tools and leaked a termination threat that damaged a potential deal with Meta Platforms
By Cris Tolomia·2 min read·Updated October 5, 2026
Qualcomm $QCOM and Arm Holdings returned to federal court in Delaware on Monday, with Qualcomm alleging that Arm refused to hand over chip testing tools owed under their contract and disclosed a termination threat to the press in a way that hurt Qualcomm's business dealings, according to Reuters.
In the lawsuit, Qualcomm is seeking to stop paying royalties to Arm for up to five years — a remedy potentially worth billions of dollars — though Judge Maryellen Noreika is weighing whether to strike that term, which would limit the damages Qualcomm could pursue, according to Reuters.
Qualcomm, one of Arm's largest customers, further claims that Arm's disclosure of the 2024 termination threat to journalists undermined ongoing chip deal negotiations with Meta $META Platforms, according to Reuters. Arm, which is owned by Japan's SoftBank Group, has rejected the breach-of-contract allegations and characterized any claimed harm to Qualcomm's chip deals as too speculative to stand. Arm has also argued that Qualcomm should be barred from recovering damages related to the leak, pointing out that Qualcomm itself disclosed confidential information about antitrust investigations involving Arm to reporters, according to Reuters.
The five-day jury trial opens a new chapter in an increasingly contentious relationship between the two companies. Running concurrently is a separate bench trial in which Judge Noreika will consider whether Arm fulfilled its duty to bargain in good faith during negotiations over the next generation of its chip architecture. That licensing agreement between the two companies remains in effect until 2033, according to the outlet.
Arm disclosed the litigation in its most recent quarterly filing, noting that Qualcomm filed the original complaint in April 2024, then amended it twice in 2025 and again in March 2026 to add additional breach-of-contract claims, including an allegation that Arm failed to negotiate certain license terms in good faith.
Qualcomm described the case in its own quarterly filing, saying its complaint seeks an order compelling Arm to fulfill its contractual obligations, damages, and other relief. Qualcomm said it has not recorded any accrual for potential losses from the matter, as it does not consider a loss probable at this time.
The companies have been entangled in litigation since 2022, when Arm sued Qualcomm alleging breach of a license agreement tied to Qualcomm's acquisition of chip startup Nuvia. A jury in December 2024 found in Qualcomm's favor on the central claims in that case, and a federal court upheld that verdict in September 2025. Arm has appealed that ruling to the United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.
Arm, long a behind-the-scenes supplier of chip design technology to companies including Qualcomm and Nvidia $NVDA, has moved in recent years to enter the chip market itself, turning former customers into rivals, according to the outlet.

The race for artificial intelligence dominance relies on both high-speed connectivity and efficient processing. Deciding whether to buy Astera Labs (ALAB +3.43%) or Arm (ARM -1.49%) depends on your appetite for growth versus stability.
Astera Labs provides specialized hardware that clears data bottlenecks in AI servers. Arm licenses the foundational blueprints used by almost every chip designer on the planet. While both benefit from the expansion of cloud computing, they offer vastly different financial profiles and risk levels for investors looking at the current landscape.
Astera Labs provides rack-scale connectivity solutions specifically designed for high-performance artificial intelligence infrastructure. As cloud providers expand their data center infrastructure, demand for specialized semiconductor stocks has intensified. The company serves major hyperscalers, but one end customer accounted for 70% of revenue in 2025, and customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.
According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached $852.5 million, representing growth of 115.1% year over year. The company reported net income of $219.1 million. This result marked a significant improvement compared with the net loss reported in the prior fiscal year.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is 10.2x, measuring the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets. Debt-to-equity is 0.0x, indicating that the company carries virtually no debt relative to shareholder equity. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 50.1% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Arm develops essential compute platforms and licenses its processor architecture to chip designers across the globe. As the digital world shifts toward more energy-efficient computing, the company's instruction set has become a global standard for everything from smartphones to servers. Its business model relies on charging royalties and licensing fees for every chip that uses its proprietary designs.
According to its latest annual report, filed for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, revenue reached $4.9 billion, a 22.8% increase compared with the prior fiscal year. Net income reached $904.0 million. Net margin, which shows the percentage of revenue turned into profit, was 18.4%.
As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is 6.0x. Debt-to-equity is 0.1x, indicating that total debt is a small fraction of shareholder equity. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Astera Labs faces significant risk from revenue concentration, as 86% of sales come from just three customers. The company also deals with intense competition from established giants like Broadcom (AVGO +2.08%) and Marvell Technology (MRVL -0.38%). Furthermore, its reliance on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +2.75%) makes it vulnerable to geopolitical instability and supply chain disruptions in East Asia.
Arm depends heavily on the continued dominance of its instruction set architecture. While it is expanding in the data center, it faces potential competition from open-source alternatives and internal designs from large cloud providers. Any shift in the licensing landscape or a slowdown in the mobile hardware market could negatively impact its royalty revenue streams.
Arm carries a significantly higher Forward P/E based on future earnings estimates than its peer, while the P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months, also favors Astera Labs.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with Astera Labs. The company has strung together one of the most impressive growth streaks in the semiconductor industry, with revenue approaching or exceeding triple digits for several consecutive quarters, gross margins above 70%, and guidance pointing to more than 85% revenue growth for the full year. Its connectivity chips are becoming essential inside the AI data centers being built by every major hyperscaler, and demand keeps outpacing expectations.
Arm has built a remarkable business model in its own right, with it architecture powering virtually every smartphone. Royalty revenue more than doubled in the data center segment, and the business compounds reliably without depending on any single product cycle. For investors who value consistency over acceleration, it is a strong long-term hold.
Customer concentration is the one risk worth watching at Astera. A handful of hyperscalers drive most of its revenue, and that makes the business sensitive to any shift in those relationships. But the demand behind those relationships keeps growing. For an investor comfortable with that trade-off, Astera's growth trajectory is simply in a different league right now.

Arm Holdings, US0420682058, Illustration mit AI erstellt.
Arm Holdings plc (ISIN US0420682058) stock is trading around USD 242.36 on Nasdaq as of September 15, 2026, recovering from a steep three-month drawdown while still far below its 52-week peak of USD 452.70 and above its 52-week low of USD 100.02.
Analysts recalibrate views on Arm Holdings stock
Analyst sentiment on Arm Holdings stock has turned more nuanced in mid-September 2026, with some houses trimming price targets while others reiterate bullish views based on Arm's position in AI infrastructure. According to Stocktwits on September 16, 2026, Wells Fargo lowered its price target for Arm from USD 410 to USD 350 while maintaining an Overweight rating, implying that the bank still sees upside potential despite moderating expectations.
In the same report, Stocktwits cites Investing.com data that Jefferies reiterated its Buy rating and raised its price target on Arm to USD 320 from USD 290, while Susquehanna lifted its target to USD 320 from USD 300 and kept a Positive rating. These moves create a spread of targets between USD 320 and USD 350, compared with the stock's recent closing level of USD 239.01 on Nasdaq as of September 15, 2026, which is roughly 46.9 percent below the Wells Fargo target and 33.9 percent below the Jefferies and Susquehanna targets.
At the same time, broader commentary classifies Arm as a Hold in light of its strong run and valuation. According to Zacks on September 20, 2026, Arm stock has declined 39 percent over the past three months but still carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), underscoring that, in their view, the shares are neither clear buys nor sells at current levels.
Upcoming Q1 earnings and recent performance metrics
The next key catalyst for Arm Holdings stock is the upcoming report of its first-quarter results. According to Stocktwits, Arm is scheduled to report Q1 results on July 29 (fiscal year 2026), with Wall Street expecting earnings per share (EPS) of USD 0.40 on revenue of USD 1.26 billion.
The same overview notes that Arm generated EPS of USD 0.35 on revenue of USD 1.05 billion in the comparable quarter a year earlier, meaning that consensus implies year-over-year revenue growth of about 20.0 percent and an EPS increase of roughly 14.3 percent if the company meets these expectations, which would signal sustained demand for its licensing and royalty model in AI and data center markets.
For investors following Arm, these Q1 expectations, if achieved or exceeded, would help justify premium valuation multiples. A research snapshot from GetStockReport on September 20, 2026, notes that Arm trades at almost triple its forward price-earnings multiple, with published analyst targets ranging from USD 125 to USD 500 depending on how fast AI data center royalties compound within Arm's high-margin licensing model. That wide target range illustrates the uncertainty around long-term growth trajectories even as near-term earnings estimates point to double-digit expansion.
Stock volatility, technical levels and year-to-date performance
Arm Holdings stock has experienced pronounced volatility in recent months, shaped both by shifting sentiment on AI-related hardware and by its own valuation resets. As of September 15, 2026, Nasdaq data compiled by MarketWatch show a prior close of USD 239.01, down USD 25.78 or 9.74 percent from the previous day, with an intraday range of USD 238.03 to USD 249.25.
Despite that drawdown, the same Stocktwits report highlights that Arm stock is up 158 percent year-to-date and 77 percent over the past 12 months as of mid-September 2026, underscoring how the recent 39 percent three-month decline documented by Zacks is occurring from an elevated base.
Technical commentary reflects this push and pull. According to a chart-based analysis from TradingKey dated September 19, 2026, Arm has broken above a downtrend line drawn from its high of USD 451.37 and reclaimed its 20-day moving average near USD 248.02. At the same time, the stock remains below its 60-day moving average around USD 273.67, and a resistance zone is described between USD 273 and USD 275, close to the 0.236 Fibonacci retracement level of USD 274.69.
The TradingKey analysis further notes that Arm's 14-day relative strength index (RSI) stands near 54, above its signal line of 46.03 but still below overbought territory, which suggests improving momentum without extreme exuberance.
Arm in the AI chip race and competitive positioning
Beyond near-term price and earnings dynamics, the strategic narrative around Arm Holdings stock centers on its role as a foundational architecture provider in AI and data center computing. A comparison piece from Yahoo Finance on September 20, 2026, contrasts Arm with SK Hynix in terms of AI exposure and notes that Arm shares recently gained about 4.04 percent in the context of broader enthusiasm for AI platforms.
An in-depth article from Yahoo Finance dated September 19, 2026, discusses whether Arm remains a hidden winner of the AI chip race, highlighting that many data center and edge devices rely on Arm-based CPU cores even when GPUs from other suppliers dominate the headlines.
The valuation discussion from GetStockReport notes that Arm's gross margins near 97 percent on licensing revenue support a capital-light, royalty-driven business model, but that the stock price already reflects high expectations for AI-driven royalty growth. The wide analyst target range between USD 125 and USD 500 captures the debate over how fast Arm's architecture will monetize AI workloads in practice.
For investors considering Arm Holdings stock, the main risk factors currently discussed revolve around valuation, competition and cyclical exposure. The Zacks note dated September 20, 2026, emphasizes that the 39 percent drop over three months comes after strong prior gains and suggests that the shares may be vulnerable to further volatility if near-term earnings disappoint or if AI spending grows more slowly than anticipated.
Additionally, the TradingKey technical analysis identifies support around USD 248 to USD 250 and warns that if Arm falls back below this zone, the recent breakout could prove false, with potential downside toward USD 235 to USD 240 or even a retest of a prior low near USD 220.11. Such scenarios would challenge the thesis embedded in higher analyst targets if they were accompanied by weaker-than-expected Q1 results.
On the other hand, if Arm meets or beats the July 29 Q1 expectations of USD 1.26 billion in revenue and USD 0.40 EPS, and if AI-related design wins continue to expand, the combination of high margins and royalty leverage could justify valuations closer to the upper end of the current target range.
Per Nasdaq data compiled by MarketWatch, Arm Holdings stock closed at USD 239.01 on Nasdaq on September 15, 2026, after an intraday range between USD 238.03 and USD 249.25, with a subsequent pre-market indication around USD 242.36. The stock's 52-week range of USD 100.02 to USD 452.70 and year-to-date gain of 158 percent underline both its growth profile and its volatility, making Arm one of the more actively debated AI infrastructure names among retail and institutional investors.

Arm Holdings (ARM) Stock Soars 7% After Nvidia AI Safety Platform News
Arm stock surged after Nvidia confirmed its chips power AI safety monitoring on BlueField 4 hardware, hitting $311.89 intraday.
By Trader EdgeOctober 2, 20263 Mins Read
Arm (ARM) stock gapped up Friday, opening at $306.78 after closing at $292.34, and trading as high as $311.89.
The rally follows news that Arm-based processors are handling AI agent execution and safety monitoring in Nvidia’s BlueField 4 hardware.
CEO Rene Haas has pointed to easing supply constraints on Arm’s AGI CPU chip and confidence in capturing $2 billion in customer demand.
Q2 earnings beat expectations, with EPS of $0.45 versus the $0.40 estimate and revenue up 22% year over year to $1.29 billion.
Analysts hold a “Moderate Buy” consensus rating, with price targets ranging from $280 to $350.
Arm Holdings stock jumped sharply on Friday. Shares opened at $306.78 after closing the prior session at $292.34.
Arm Holdings plc American Depositary Shares, ARM
By midday trading, ARM had climbed as high as $311.89. That’s a strong move even by this stock’s volatile standards.
The spark came from Nvidia. The chipmaker confirmed that Arm-based processors are running both AI agent execution and safety monitoring on its new BlueField 4 hardware.
This matters because it shows Arm’s chip designs moving well beyond smartphones. AI infrastructure is now a real growth lane for the company.
Arm’s last earnings report, released July 30th, gave bulls plenty to work with. EPS came in at $0.45, beating the $0.40 estimate analysts had penciled in.
Revenue reached $1.29 billion for the quarter. That’s a 22% jump from the same period last year.
CEO Rene Haas has also been talking up the company’s AGI CPU chip. He’s said supply constraints are easing and that Arm is on track to capture the full $2 billion in identified customer demand.
That combination, a clean earnings beat plus a loosening supply picture, has helped fuel a roughly 20% rebound for the stock since September. Worth noting: ARM had nearly cut its value in half from its June peak before that bounce began.
Not everyone is fully on board, though. TD Cowen trimmed its price target from $475 to $350 in late July, even while keeping a buy rating.
Wells Fargo cut its target too, moving from $350 down to $280, though it kept an overweight rating attached.
Piper Sandler took the opposite approach. The firm initiated coverage with an Overweight rating, citing server CPU design wins and hyperscaler partnerships as reasons to stay optimistic long-term.
Across the board, one analyst rates ARM a Strong Buy, eighteen say Buy, seven say Hold, and one has it at Sell. The consensus price target sits at $303.32.
There’s also been some insider selling to note. CFO Jason Child sold 10,400 shares on September 21st at an average price of $300.00, a transaction worth $3.12 million.
That sale was done under a pre-arranged trading plan, not a snap decision. Child still holds 153,442 shares after the sale.
Institutional investors have been active too. Hyperion Asset Management grew its stake by 28% last quarter, now holding over 1.8 million shares worth more than $200 million.
Capital Research Global Investors added to its position as well, lifting its stake by 5.1%. Franklin Resources also increased its holdings slightly during the same period.
The stock’s valuation remains on the pricier side. ARM trades at a P/E ratio of 324, with a market cap around $335.7 billion.
Arm’s 50-day moving average sits at $264.70, while its 200-day average is $259.93. Both are well below Friday’s trading levels, underscoring just how sharp this recent move has been.

As the demand for high-performance computing accelerates, investors often struggle to choose between the architects of chip design and the manufacturers of chipmaking hardware. Choosing between Arm (ARM -1.49%) and ASML (ASML -0.40%) requires understanding their distinct roles.
Arm licenses its intellectual property to hundreds of companies, earning royalties on nearly every smartphone sold globally. Meanwhile, ASML provides the essential machinery that allows foundries to print those designs onto silicon. Both companies are vital players among semiconductor stocks, but they offer different paths to growth.
Arm operates a high-margin business model centered on licensing its compute platform and central processing unit designs. The company provides the fundamental blueprints that power the mobile world and is increasingly gaining traction in the automotive and cloud data center sectors. Because it does not manufacture physical chips, its asset-light model allows it to scale across the entire industry without the heavy costs of factory ownership.
In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $4.9 billion, representing growth of approximately 22.8% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company reported a net income of roughly $904.0 million for the period. While its net margin of approximately 18.4% was slightly lower than the previous year, the company continues to see strong adoption of its latest architecture versions.
As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio stands at approximately 6.0x, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term liabilities with its short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, is roughly 0.1x. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
ASML occupies a unique position as the sole provider of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines. These massive, highly complex tools are the only way for chipmakers to produce the smallest and most advanced transistors. This technological moat makes the company an indispensable partner for any foundry aiming to support modern artificial intelligence applications.
In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached nearly $37.1 billion, a growth of approximately 15.6% over the prior fiscal year. The company achieved a net income of close to $10.9 billion for the year. This resulted in a healthy net margin of approximately 29.4%, reflecting the premium pricing power that comes with its specialized equipment monopoly.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 1.3x. Its debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.1x, suggesting a conservative use of leverage relative to its equity. The company generated approximately $12.1 billion in free cash flow, which is the cash remaining after a business pays for its operating expenses and capital expenditures.
Arm faces risks related to the concentration of its architecture in the mobile market, where growth has slowed compared to earlier decades. The company also contends with the rise of open-source alternatives like RISC-V, which could eventually challenge its licensing dominance. Additionally, geopolitical tensions can impact its ability to license technology in certain sensitive regions, potentially limiting its total addressable market.
ASML is highly sensitive to the capital expenditure cycles of a few major chip manufacturers. If these customers delay their expansion plans, the company's hardware orders can experience significant volatility. Furthermore, international trade restrictions on advanced lithography tools, particularly regarding shipments to certain markets, remain a persistent challenge that could cap its long-term revenue potential.
ASML appears significantly cheaper on a relative basis when comparing both its premium to earnings and its valuation relative to total sales.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with ASML. Its position in the semiconductor industry is one of the most defensible in the world: It is the only company that makes the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines needed to produce the most advanced chips. Every chipmaker building AI hardware depends on ASML's equipment to do it, and there is no alternative. That kind of irreplaceable role in the global technology supply chain is extraordinarily rare.
There is a lot to like about how Arm makes its money. Its architecture powers virtually every smartphone, and royalty revenue more than doubled in the data center segment. This is a business that compounds reliably without depending on any single product cycle. For investors who value consistency and steady growth, it is a strong long-term hold.
Both companies benefit from the AI build-out, but from different angles. Arm earns a royalty when a chip is designed, while ASML earns revenue when that chip gets built. But as chip demand keeps growing, ASML sits at the only chokepoint in the entire supply chain that cannot be worked around. For a long-term investor, that is a compelling place to put your money.

Arm Holdings PLC Sponsored ADR (ISIN US0420682058) stock closed at USD 264.90 on Nasdaq on September 17, 2026, up 8.6% from the prior close as investors reacted to CEO Rene Haas highlighting a path to about USD 2 billion in demand for the company’s new AGI CPU artificial intelligence chip in fiscal years 2027 and 2028.
According to Invezz on September 17, 2026, CEO Rene Haas said he was increasingly confident Arm can meet Wall Street’s higher revenue expectations, pointing to roughly USD 2 billion in anticipated demand for its AGI CPU data center chip across fiscal years 2027 and 2028.
As Yahoo Finance reported on September 18, 2026, shares of Arm Holdings jumped 8.57% on September 17 after Haas said he believes the semiconductor designer is on track to generate USD 2 billion from its new artificial intelligence chip.
From a broader sector perspective, Arm’s move came amid a rebound in US chip stocks, with the company’s shares rising 8.57 percent alongside strong gains for peers in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index on September 17, 2026, as noted by Yahoo Finance on September 18, 2026.
Arm’s latest reported quarter underpins the CEO’s confidence. According to MarketBeat on September 17, 2026, Arm recently exceeded quarterly expectations by reporting earnings per share of USD 0.45 and revenue of USD 1.29 billion in its most recent quarter, beating consensus estimates.
The same MarketBeat overview notes that Arm’s price-to-earnings ratio stood at about 269.09 based on that quarter’s figures as of mid-September 2026, highlighting a rich valuation compared with many peers.
For investors, the revenue surprise in the latest quarter is tangible: revenue reached USD 1.29 billion, and the company delivered USD 0.45 in EPS, both ahead of analyst expectations for that reporting period, according to the MarketBeat data.
In addition to the earnings beat, the CEO’s focus on transforming Arm from a traditional intellectual property licensor into a direct data center chip supplier is central to the strategy. As TradingKey outlined on September 18, 2026, the prospective USD 2 billion AGI CPU demand would complement Arm’s existing surging server royalty revenues and deepen its role in AI data centers.
Analyst targets and sentiment remain supportive
Analysts remain broadly positive on Arm Holdings stock despite the recent volatility. According to MarketBeat on September 17, 2026, Arm carries a consensus rating of Moderate Buy, with an average analyst price target of USD 305.72, and individual targets ranging roughly from USD 212 to USD 500.
In the same period, Bernstein analyst David Dai maintained a buy rating but trimmed his price target from USD 500 to USD 480, as reported by Invezz on September 17, 2026.
The shift from USD 500 to USD 480 still implies notable upside of about 81 percent from the September 17, 2026 closing price of USD 264.90, while the broader consensus of USD 305.72 suggests a more moderate potential gain of around 15 percent from that close.
Other analyst commentary remains constructive. As MarketBeat notes, Piper Sandler initiated coverage on Arm with an Overweight rating and a USD 320 price objective in early September 2026, underscoring confidence in the company’s longer-term AI and data center opportunity set.
Looking at the dispersion of targets, data summarized by MarketBeat on September 17, 2026 indicate that the consensus target around USD 305.72 sits between cautious estimates near USD 212 and bullish calls as high as USD 500, reflecting differing views on how quickly Arm can convert its AI momentum into sustained earnings growth.
SoftBank’s margin loan and ownership concentration add a risk layer
Arm’s stock story is also tightly linked to its majority shareholder, SoftBank Group Corp. According to The Edge Malaysia on September 18, 2026, SoftBank increased a margin loan backed by Arm shares by USD 5 billion to USD 25 billion as it seeks funding for expanding artificial intelligence investments.
The same report highlights that the enlarged margin loan is secured by a large stake in Arm Holdings and that Arm’s share price has risen about 142 percent year to date, which supports the collateral value but also raises questions about leverage and potential selling pressure if markets turn.
Complementing that picture, commentary aggregated by 24/7 Wall St via Ground News on September 18, 2026 notes that SoftBank beneficially owns more than 80 percent of Arm and that a significant block of shares has been pledged, which could influence the stock’s floor and ceiling if SoftBank alters its stance or is forced to adjust its financing.
For shareholders, this concentration means that Arm’s free float is relatively limited compared with many S&P 500 technology names, and large moves in the stock can be amplified by SoftBank-related transactions, even as the company’s operating performance and AI roadmap remain the fundamental drivers.
Technical picture after the breakout move
Technically, the September 17, 2026 rally has shifted Arm’s chart structure. As TradingKey analyzed on September 18, 2026, the stock broke above a downtrend line drawn from its June 2026 high of about USD 451.37 and reclaimed its 20 day moving average, which sits near USD 248.02.
The same technical review points out that daily trading volume rose to roughly 6.11 million shares during the breakout, providing volume confirmation for the move, while the 14 day relative strength index climbed to around 54, indicating strengthening buying interest without entering overbought territory.
Despite the improvement, resistance remains. According to TradingKey, the 60 day moving average around USD 273.67 and a Fibonacci retracement level near USD 274.69 together form a key resistance zone between USD 273 and USD 275, with the after hours price around USD 268.60 still below that band as of September 18, 2026.
For short term traders, the analysis suggests that holding above the USD 248 to USD 250 support area is important to maintain the bullish structure, while a sustained break above USD 275 on higher volume could open a path toward the USD 300 to USD 305 region referenced by both technical projections and the average analyst price target.
Even after the September 17, 2026 surge, Arm Holdings stock trades well below its earlier peak. Invezz notes that Arm shares remain about 45 percent below their June 2026 high of roughly USD 452, even after holding onto the July post earnings gains, which frames the current price around USD 264.90 as both a recovery and a discount to previous exuberant levels.
That gap between the current level and the June high means the stock would need to gain roughly 82 percent to revisit the USD 452 area, underscoring the scale of upside implied by the most bullish price targets in the market while also highlighting the risk if AI demand or execution falls short of management’s ambitions.
Arm Holdings stock price and market data
Per data summarized by MarketBeat on September 17, 2026, Arm Holdings stock had previously closed at USD 243.98 on Nasdaq and then gapped up to open around USD 262.00, trading intraday near USD 261.73 before ending the session at USD 264.90. That move represents a gain of about 8.6 percent in a single trading day.
The same data show that intraday the stock traded as high as USD 267.00, with around 6,077,201 shares changing hands compared with an average session volume of roughly 7,765,334 shares, indicating strong but not extreme participation in the rally.
On a trailing basis, commentary collated by 24/7 Wall St via Ground News on September 18, 2026 notes that Arm shares were up about 123.2 percent year to date and roughly 142 percent over a comparable period, reflecting substantial gains driven by enthusiasm for AI related revenue streams and recurring royalty income.
For investors assessing the risk reward, the combination of a steep year to date advance, a valuation multiple above 250 times recent earnings, and a large margin loan backed by the majority shareholder’s stake reinforces the importance of the CEO’s USD 2 billion AGI CPU demand target and the company’s ability to deliver on that roadmap over fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

As artificial intelligence reshapes the global economy, investors can decide between the foundational architecture of Arm Holdings (ARM -1.49%) and the powerhouse performance of NVIDIA (NVDA +2.12%) to anchor their portfolios for 2026.
Arm designs the underlying blueprints used in nearly every smartphone, while NVIDIA builds the massive graphics processors that power modern data centers. While both are critical players in the chip market, they occupy very different niches in the technology value chain.
Arm develops the compute platform behind energy-efficient CPU products, making it a leader among semiconductor stocks. Its technology is currently deployed in more than 350 billion chips, providing the architecture for over 99% of the world's smartphones. The company also targets high-growth markets such as cloud computing, networking, automotive, and the internet of things.
In its 2026 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $4.9 billion, representing growth of 22.8% compared to the previous year. This expansion was supported by a net income of $904.0 million. The company reported a net margin of 18.4%, reflecting a slight decrease from the 19.8% net margin recorded in the prior fiscal year.
As of its March 2026 balance sheet, Arm maintained a current ratio of roughly 6.0x, indicating a strong ability to cover short-term liabilities with its current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.1x, which compares total debt to the amount of equity held by shareholders. Free cash flow for the period was $979 million. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
NVIDIA is a full-stack artificial intelligence infrastructure company that serves gaming, professional visualization, and data center markets. In its latest annual report, the company disclosed that two direct customers accounted for 22% and 14% of its FY 2026 revenue. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. Beyond hardware, NVIDIA has expanded its software ecosystem through material developments like the $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face. The company also maintains a long-standing agreement with Microsoft (MSFT +1.48%) regarding Xbox and data center infrastructure support.
In FY 2026, revenue reached $215.9 billion, which is a massive 65.5% increase over the $130.5 billion reported in FY 2025. This growth translated into a net income of $120.1 billion. The company achieved an exceptional net margin of 55.6%, a level of profitability that remained remarkably stable compared to the 55.8% net margin seen in the previous year.
Based on its January 2026 balance sheet, NVIDIA carries a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.1x, suggesting a conservative use of borrowed funds relative to shareholder equity. Its current ratio of 3.9x shows that the company has ample liquidity to meet its short-term financial obligations. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was $96.7 billion. Free cash flow measures the cash a company generates after accounting for the money spent on equipment and infrastructure.
Arm faces competition from established players like Intel (INTC -2.63%) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -0.34%), as it tries to gain ground in the data center market. The company also faces risks related to its heavy dependence on the mobile device industry, which can be cyclical. Furthermore, the rise of open-source architectures may provide a low-cost alternative to its licensing model, potentially affecting its ability to maintain its high royalty rates in certain segments.
NVIDIA faces severe operational constraints due to evolving U.S. export controls, particularly those affecting the data center segment in China. The company relies on a fabless manufacturing model heavily concentrated with partners in Asia, exposing it to geopolitical tensions. Additionally, NVIDIA is subject to various international antitrust inquiries and a certified class action securities lawsuit. The rapid pace of product transitions, such as the Blackwell architecture, also presents risks related to potential inventory impairments if demand estimates are inaccurate.
NVIDIA appears significantly more attractive on a Forward P/E basis, whereas Arm's high P/S ratio reflects a much steeper premium.
Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Arm Holdings and NVIDIA are great stocks for investors seeking exposure to the hot artificial intelligence sector. Both possess dominant market positions in their respective technologies. However, between the two, I would buy NVIDIA shares.
Certainly, Arm is poised to see further revenue growth. Its new designs to support AI in mobile devices coupled with its expansion into data centers and physical AI systems, such as robots, will fuel future sales.
That said, NVIDIA's secret weapon is its CEO and founder, Jensen Huang. He has successfully anticipated where the AI industry is going over the past several years. From Huang's work years ago with OpenAI to build computing tech specifically for artificial intelligence to his prediction of AI factories that has led to a massive data center buildout around the globe, his vision and leadership has enabled NVIDIA to post exceptional financial performance.
For its next act, the company is working on a platform to support quantum computers. Add to this NVIDIA's far more attractive share price valuation, and this is the stock with the greater upside potential.

Last month, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates by 0.25% to a target range of 3/75% to 4.00%. The decision marked the first rate hike in three years, reversing prior cuts.
"Earnings don't move the overall market; it's the Federal Reserve Board…focus on the Central banks and focus on the movement of liquidity." ~Stanley Druckenmiller
Monitoring the Fed's next monetary policy is absolutely critical for investors as Fed liquidity (or lack thereof) is the biggest driver of equity prices. Despite the Fed's "hawkish" rate hike last month, mounting evidence suggests Warsh and the Fed will NOT hike rates again at the October 27-28 meeting. Below are 5 reasons why:
1. Jobs Market Weakens: Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unveiled lackluster jobs numbers. July and August hiring numbers were revised downward by a combined 60,000 jobs, erasing earlier perceived strength.
2. Hawkish Fed Speak: Two top Fed officials, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and Federal Reserve Bank of New York CEO John C. Williams, recently hinted that there is no current urgency for the Fed to deliver another rate hike.
3. Betting Markets:Rate-hike odds plunged recently on popular betting markets. For instance, on Polymarket, the odds of an October rate hike plunged from 69% to just 17%.
4. October Rate Hike Pre-Midterm Is Unprecedented: Recent history favors the Doves. Since 1990, the Fed has never hiked interest rates when it met in October ahead of a midterm election in November.
5. Government Inflation #s Lag: Government inflation numbers are notoriously stale. Truflation offers a more up-to-date inflation number. According to Truflation, CPI is at 2.77%, much lower than the government's reported 3.4% and closer to the Fed's target.
What Does this Mean for Investors?
Rate hike cycles are not necessarily blanketly bearish. The difference between a bullish and bearish rate-hike cyckle is the pace of hikes. In other words, if the slower the rate of hikes, the more bullish it is for equities. Today, stocks are reflecting this notion as AI leaders such as Arm Holdings, Advanced Micro Devices, Marvell Technologies, Applied Optoelectronics and Nebius Group jump.
Monitoring the Fed's next policy shift remains crucial as market liquidity dictates equity momentum. The overwhelming evidence suggests an October pause is in order.

Will Selling Chips Strengthen Arm’s Moat or Put It at Risk?
Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ:ARM) built its business around helping other companies design processors. Selling its own data-center CPU gives it a chance to capture more revenue from each system, but changes its relationship with the same customers that license its technology. Investors need to decide whether that change enlarges the moat or makes it more expensive to maintain.
NVIDIA sold its Arm shares while continuing to use Arm's architecture. Our analysis asks what that split between ownership and dependence means for Arm's moat. The chip strategy also puts Arm closer to the hardware economics examined in our analysis of how abundant AI capacity could shift bargaining power toward chip customers.
Will Selling Chips Strengthen Arm's Moat or Put It at Risk?
For illustration purposes only. Photo from Arm Holdings
A bigger revenue opportunity brings different costs
In its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results, released July 29, Arm reported $1.29 billion of revenue. Royalties contributed $715 million, up 22%, and licensing and other revenue $574 million, up 23%. Data-center royalty revenue more than doubled. That gives the chip program a growing base rather than a stagnant business it must rescue.
Arm said its AGI CPU had been delivered to initial customers and that it had secured capacity for a $1 billion revenue opportunity across fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028. Management described demand exceeding $2 billion over those two years. The latter figure is demand commentary, not recognized revenue or a guaranteed order book. Even the smaller capacity-backed opportunity spans two years, making it inappropriate to compare directly with one quarter's revenue.
Licensing lets customers bear much of the manufacturing, inventory and product-commercialization burden. Selling chips can capture more dollars, but Arm must participate more directly in those costs. Revenue growth therefore needs to be tested against incremental gross profit and cash investment. A chip dollar and a royalty dollar are not interchangeable valuation units.
Insider Monkey's hedge fund database showed 52 Arm holders in Q2 2026, compared with 46 in Q1, an increase of six. That historical participation says little about the eventual economics of the chip initiative.
A large multiple needs more than a successful launch
At the September 30 market-data snapshot, Arm traded at roughly 59 times enterprise value to trailing revenue and about 205 times trailing free cash flow. Those measures price in substantial expansion. The reported first-quarter revenue, annualized mechanically, would be $5.16 billion; it is a run-rate illustration rather than an annual forecast.
Against the approximately $306 billion enterprise value in the snapshot, a future $10 billion revenue business at a 30% operating margin would generate $3 billion of operating profit and still be valued at more than 100 times that profit. At $15 billion of revenue and a 40% margin, the equivalent multiple would be around 51. Both scenarios require assumptions about scale and business mix; neither is management guidance. They show why a new product opportunity cannot, by itself, explain the current valuation.
Arm had 15,521,694 shares sold short at the September 15 settlement, with 3.9 days to cover. Its relatively small publicly traded float makes the denominator important; a percentage calculated against all outstanding shares would understate public-float exposure.
The best bull case is broader than direct chip sales. Arm can earn royalties from customers' processors while using its own product to accelerate the architecture's adoption and demonstrate competitive performance. Continued growth in licensing and royalties would support that interpretation.
The bear case is a gradual erosion of neutrality. A customer may become less willing to share its roadmap or depend on a supplier that also competes for the same server budget. There is no basis here to claim that customers have already defected. The risk becomes investment-relevant if the chip business expands while licensing growth, customer breadth or royalty economics weaken.
Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ:ARM) can expand its opportunity by selling competitive data-center systems. Its stock case improves when that expansion produces incremental cash profit while licensing and royalties keep growing. A larger chip business accompanied by weaker customer licensing or heavier capital demands would change the moat calculation.
While we acknowledge the potential of ARM as an investment, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Qualcomm Takes Arm to Court Over Withheld Chip Testing Tools and Leaked Deal Threats
Qualcomm Takes Arm to Court Over Withheld Chip Testing Tools and Leaked Deal Threats ©@Madmaxer from Getty Images via Canva, @Vedat OGUZCAN from Getty Images via Canva
Price change for Arm Holdings stock in the last 6 months: 107%
What Happened?
Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) is back in court with one of its biggest customers. Qualcomm and Arm face off on Monday in a five-day jury trial. It is being held in a U.S. federal court in Delaware.
Qualcomm makes two main claims.
First, it says Arm withheld chip-testing tools due under their contract.
Second, it says Arm leaked its 2024 threat to end a key license deal.
Qualcomm says the leak hurt talks for a chip deal with Meta.
Qualcomm wants to stop paying royalties to Arm for up to five years. That could be worth billions of dollars.
But Judge Maryellen Noreika is deciding whether to throw out that part of the contract. If she does, Qualcomm could only seek smaller damages.
ARM Stock Revenue, EBIT and Free Cash Flow Estimates in Billion USD (TIKR)
Arm denies breaking the contract. It calls the claims of damage to Qualcomm's deals speculative.
Arm also says Qualcomm can't seek damages over the leak. It says Qualcomm leaked private details of antitrust probes into Arm.
The judge will also hear a related bench trial. It covers whether Arm negotiated in good faith on the next version of its chip technology.
Qualcomm's agreement with Arm runs through 2033.
What the Market Is Telling Us About Arm Holdings Stock
This fight has a long history. Arm sued Qualcomm in 2022. Qualcomm won a key victory in 2024. Now it's on offense.
The risk to Arm Holdings stock is about money and trust. Royalties are Arm's largest revenue line. Royalty revenue was $715 million last quarter, up 22%.
It made up more than half of total revenue of $1.29 billion. Losing years of Qualcomm royalties would be a real hit. Still, the judge may limit the damages.
The business itself looks healthy. Licensing revenue was $574 million, up 23%. Non-GAAP EPS was $0.45. Free cash flow was $665 million.
Arm guided next quarter revenue to about $1.38 billion.
There is also a new twist.
Arm now sells its own chips, the Arm AGI CPU. On the Q1 call, management said demand is above $2 billion. Qualcomm is also entering data center CPUs. That makes Arm a customer and a rival.
For investors, the trial adds a headline risk for Arm Holdings stock. The outcome could affect future talks between the two firms.
Still, Arm Holdings stock is also driven by data center growth, where royalties more than doubled last quarter.
Watch the ruling on the royalty term first. That decision could matter most for Arm Holdings stock.

Arm Holdings Stock Closed Above Wall Street’s $289 Target. Here’s the Margin Math That Decides What Comes Next
Arm Holdings Stock Closed Above Wall Street's $289 Target. Here's the Margin Math That Decides What Comes Next ©@Quality Stock Arts via Canva, @cyber motherboard microchip from pedrovenancio72 via Canva
What Happened?
Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) closed at $307.49 on October 2, 2026, up 5.18% during a broad rally in chip and tech stocks. That left shares up 181% year to date and above the Street's mean target of around $289. They remain below the $322.90 close of September 21. That day's chip rally, which coverage linked to Meta Platforms' (META) Muse AI agent, lifted Meta 11.4% and Arm 17.2%, though Meta has not said whose processors run Muse.
Behind the run sits a quieter shift. Royalties brought in $715 million of Arm's $1.29 billion in revenue for the June quarter, results Arm reported on July 29 and posted in its investor relations materials. The new AGI CPU, however, earns a fraction of royalty margins.
A Doubled 2031 Forecast Meets High-30s Gross Margins
As of October 4, consensus revenue for fiscal 2031, which ends in March 2031, stood around $26 billion, up from around $12 billion at the end of 2025. The analysts covering that year rose from 3 to 11 over the same span, so the two averages are not like-for-like. On the July 29 call, an analyst cited $15 billion of AGI CPU revenue expected for fiscal 2031. CEO Rene Haas said Arm is "not changing the numbers at all," adding that its March market-size view "may have been conservative."
Those chips earn far less per dollar of sales. Jason Child, Arm's Chief Financial Officer, said first-generation AGI CPU gross margin should be "somewhere in the high 30% range, maybe low 40s percent," with 50% expected over "the next couple of years." Street estimates show Arm's gross margin falling from 98.2% in fiscal 2026 to around 70% in fiscal 2031. Normalized net margin is still forecast to rise from 38.4% to around 44%. In other words, the Street is counting on operating leverage to absorb a roughly 28-point gross margin drop.
Nvidia's Agent Watchdog Runs on Arm Server Cores
The royalty side shows up in less obvious places. On September 28, Nvidia (NVDA) launched its Open Agent Safety Platform, with Arm among its backers. Its Sentry watchdog, offered as a reference design, runs on BlueField-4 data processing units.
BlueField-4, unveiled in 2025, swaps BlueField-3's up to 16 Cortex-A78 cores, a design typically marketed for smartphones, for a 64-core Grace CPU built on Arm's server-grade Neoverse V2. The platform's OpenShell software can also run on Intel (INTC) x86 systems, and Arm does not disclose what it earns per DPU.
Child pointed to that pocket on the call: "This is being driven by the continued ramp of Arm-based server chips at all the major hyperscalers alongside increasing deployments of data center networking chips, particularly DPUs and SmartNICs where Arm technology is deployed in nearly all leading products." Neoverse shipments passed 1.5 billion cores, with the latest 500 million arriving in 9 months versus 6 years for the first 1 billion.
Higher memory prices pushed Child's fiscal 2027 royalty growth estimate to "closer to the high teens" from about 20%, and Q2 royalty growth is guided to 13%. He expects royalties back "in that 20% range next year and beyond."
At about 129 times NTM normalized earnings, versus about 71 times for Intel and a peer median near 65 times, the stock needs both businesses working. Of 43 ratings, 21 are Buy, 8 Outperform, 12 Hold, and 2 Sell.
Arm Holdings Advanced Valuation Model (TIKR)
The mid case is TIKR's central scenario, so it gives the fairest read on whether a buyer at $307.49 still gets paid. It targets around $1,375 by March 31, 2031, about 40% a year over 4.5 years. For context only, and not as the model's inputs, Street consensus has revenue compounding around 39% a year, from $4.92 billion in fiscal 2026 to around $26 billion in fiscal 2031.
The main risk is supply, which Child called "pretty tight" through calendar 2027. Upside would come from a CPU market nearer the "up to $200 billion" some peers have floated, double Arm's own roughly $100 billion view. Downside would come from royalties stalling while silicon dilutes margins faster than scale offsets it.
Arm's investor site lists November 4, 2026, as a tentative date for fiscal Q2 results. Royalty growth at or above the 13% guide would show the high-margin engine holding while the AGI CPU ramps. The larger checkpoint is fiscal 2028, when Child expects silicon to reach 10% of revenue and become its own reporting line. At that point, the lower-margin business will be visible in plain numbers.

Arm Holdings (ARM) Could Be 34% Undervalued On Its AI Growth Narrative
Tue, September 29, 2026 at 2:09 AM PDT 3 min read
Arm Holdings (NasdaqGS:ARM) is back in focus as investors digest a sharp pullback in the share price following sector wide pressure on chipmakers and fresh concern around AI model safety.
In the short term, momentum has cooled, with a 1-day share price return of 8.70% and a 7-day share price return of 12.25% both moving lower as bond yields, AI safety worries and sector wide selling hit chipmakers. Yet Arm Holdings still carries a 30-day share price return of 18.52%, a year to date share price return of 146.95% and a 1-year total shareholder return of 102.67%. The 3-year total shareholder return of 442.15% shows earlier gains remain substantial even after recent volatility.

It already dominates smartphones, is gaining share in data centers, benefits from royalty-rate expansion, and now has a potentially transformational AGI CPU opportunity. If management's FY2031 framework proves even broadly accurate, Arm can grow from a ~$5B revenue company into a ~$25B platform business.

Arm Holdings Stock Fell 8% in a Day. Here’s What SoftBank’s $25 Billion Loan Means for the Stock
Arm Holdings Stock Fell 8% in a Day. Here's What SoftBank's $25 Billion Loan Means for the Stock ©@Tim Girard from Tim Girard's Images via Canva, @Aleksandr Grechanyuk from Getty Images via Canva
What Happened?
Arm Holdings (ARM) fell 7.88% on September 24 to close at $306.34, and the drop had more to do with Arm than the flat market around it. The Nasdaq finished the session essentially unchanged, so this was not a broad growth-stock selloff. Two Arm-specific pressures did the work: a retracement of the stock's roughly 15% Meta Muse spike from September 21, and renewed focus on a CFO share sale disclosed days earlier, both landing on a valuation priced for perfection at more than 300 times trailing earnings.
What makes this drop different from the selloffs earlier in the year is who else is now exposed to it. Days before, on September 18, SoftBank increased a margin loan backed by its Arm shares to $25 billion from $20 billion. Arm's majority owner has tied its own borrowing capacity to Arm's share price, so a stock already priced for perfection now carries a second sensitivity that has nothing to do with royalties or AI chips.
SoftBank Turned Arm's Price Into Its Own Collateral
SoftBank owns about 86% of Arm, and it is funding an enormous AI spending campaign, anchored by a multibillion-dollar investment in OpenAI. To raise cash without selling Arm stock, it has leaned on a margin loan secured by that stake, and this month it renegotiated the facility up to $25 billion, as first reported byBloomberg. Lenders reportedly offered more than SoftBank sought, a sign banks are comfortable taking Arm shares as collateral at current prices.
Margin loans carry loan-to-value limits, so a sharp drop in the collateral can shrink the borrowing base or trigger a call that forces selling. That creates a feedback loop the stock did not have a year ago: an Arm decline pressures SoftBank's funding math, which can invite more selling, which pressures Arm again. It changes nothing about the operating business, but it adds technical fragility on top of an already extreme valuation. The governance backdrop adds to the unease, with proxy advisers ISS and Glass Lewis both recommending a vote against a plan that could pay CEO Rene Haas up to $800 million if Arm reaches a $2 trillion valuation.
In its most recent quarter (fiscal Q1 2027, reported July 29), revenue rose 22% year-over-year to a record $1.29 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.45 beat both guidance and the $0.40 Street estimate. Data center royalty revenue more than doubled year-over-year again, and Neoverse cores have crossed 1.5 billion shipped, the most recent 500 million in nine months against six years for the first billion.
The order book behind the new AGI CPU, Arm's first in-house data center chip, now exceeds $2 billion against $1 billion of committed supply, and management says confidence in beating that $1 billion has risen. Getting the chips built is the harder part. CEO Rene Haas described the constraint bluntly on the July call: "It is a very, very, very tight market across everything, whether it's memory, whether it's test equipment, whether it's substrates, whether it's TSMC wafers." That tightness is why the pipeline outruns bookable revenue, and it delays the exact chip sales the valuation counts on.
The other soft spot is smartphones. Higher memory prices are squeezing handsets, and CFO Jason Child walked full-year royalty growth down toward the high teens from roughly 20%. The mature business is cooling just as the growth business inflects. The CFO share sale that traders fixated on was routine: a pre-scheduled Rule 10b5-1 disposal worth about $3.12 million that left Child with more than 150,000 shares.
Even after the drop, Arm trades near 312 times trailing earnings and about 128 times forward earnings, aprice-to-earnings ratio unmatched in its group, against a semiconductor peer set whose forward P/E averages roughly 67 times on TIKR's Competitors page. Rambus sits near 31 times, and even fast-growing Global Unichip trades near 108. Arm is priced as a separate asset class, and that price is a forecast about the next five years.
The one piece of support is that the Street's mean target of $288.71 now sits just below the market price, a reversal from the summer when the stock traded far above it. Over the past year, that configuration has tended to mark resets rather than tops. Whether it repeats depends on execution Arm has promised but not yet put in the income statement, and the stock now has to clear both the valuation bar and the leverage overhang at once.
Arm Holdings NTM Price / Normalized Earnings (P/E) (TIKR)
Arm Holdings Advanced Valuation Model (TIKR)
The TIKR model uses the mid-case scenario, a long-horizon view rather than a next-year call. It points to a price near $1,368 by early 2031, roughly 346% total return, or about 39% annualized over four and a half years. Nothing about today's multiple makes Arm cheap; the case rests entirely on where the business goes.
Two drivers carry the revenue line: the data center royalty ramp, as Neoverse adoption widens across every major hyperscaler, and the AGI CPU, a merchant-silicon stream Arm has never had, now backed by a pipeline above $2 billion. The margin driver is the mix shift toward Armv9 and compute subsystems, which carry higher royalty rates. On mid-case assumptions, revenue compounds near 50% with net margin in the mid-40s.
The primary risk is the multiple itself, and the model bakes in high-single-digit annual P/E compression, so earnings growth has to outrun a shrinking multiple. The upside case is that AGI CPU demand keeps running ahead of its $2 billion pipeline and pulls the timeline forward. The downside case is heavier now than a month ago: a phone-royalty business still paying for an AI story it cannot yet monetize, with a parent whose funding tightens every time the stock falls.
Two things now decide this stock, and only one is about Arm. The first is royalty growth: the next report, fiscal second quarter results due November 4, is guided to revenue near $1.38 billion with royalty growth in the low teens, and it tells you whether the data center engine is offsetting the smartphone drag. …Watch the royalty line when the September quarter reports in November, and watch how Arm trades on the next macro shock. A business beating its guide while the stock swings on leverage and collateral math would say the market is pricing the parent's balance sheet.
Should You Invest in Arm Holdings?
The only way to really know is to look at the numbers yourself. TIKR gives you free access to the same institutional-quality financial data that professional analysts use to answer exactly that question.
